Learning Objectives
Identify appropriate imaging modalities for the evaluation of spinal maladies.
Critically analyze and correlate imaging findings with physical examination findings.
Recognize the limitations and advantages of various imaging modalities for the spine.

strengths, and limitations. Orthopaedists must be able to order and analyze appropriate

Imaging Modalities
Radiography
Radiography is the first-line imaging modality for the assessment of spinal pathology. (Figure
1)

Radiography
Conventional radiography relies ionizing radiation to differentiate tissues with varying
absorption capacities. Bone and other calcium-rich tissues absorb x-rays more efficiently
than soft tissues with a higher water content, producing a higher signal on the detector.1
Radiography is the first-line imaging modality for the assessment of spinal pathology, if
deemed necessary. Current recommendations for patients with acute low back pain or
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
3/30

neck pain without red-flag symptoms suggest a 4- to 6-week course of nonsurgical
treatment before plain radiographs are obtained.2 Radiographs should be obtained in
patients who sustained trauma and have axial spine pain to ensure fractures are not
missed. Conventional radiography is associated with several advantages. Conventional
radiography is commonly is available in inpatient, outpatient, emergency room, and
urgent care settings. Radiographs can be obtained quickly and are cost effective. In
addition, radiography exposes patients to relatively low doses of radiation. The ease of
obtaining radiographs and their low morbidity makes radiography ideal for the initial
evaluation of acute spine pathology and for routine preoperative and postoperative
assessment. In addition, portable, low-dose radiation fluoroscopy has become popular
for guided injections, intraoperative localization, instrumentation, and deformity
correction. Dissimilar to CT and MRI, which comprise many individually viewed images,
radiographs provide a complete representation of spinal bony architecture and global
alignment.1 The ability to obtain radiographs in various patient positions and with
manipulation, such as flexion-extension, lateral bending, and traction, is especially
useful. Despite the popularity of radiography, surgeons must recognize its limitations.
Soft tissues of the spine, including ligaments, neural elements, intervertebral disks, fluid
collections, and tumors, are poorly visualized. In addition, bone density changes are not
observed on radiographs until a loss of 30% to 50% of bony architecture occurs.3
Radiographic bony changes from infection may not be observed for up to 8 weeks. The
quality of radiographs is operator and patient dependent. Often, radiographs may be
inadequate because of patient positioning, especially in the lower cervical spine region.
Although the ability to alter patient positioning may be advantageous, incorrect patient
positioning, poor posture, and unrecognized compensation may result in images that
should be interpreted with caution.
AP and lateral radiographs of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine are commonly
obtained. The AP view allows for visualization of the transverse processes, pedicle size,
coronal alignment, and rotation via the spinous processes. The lateral view affords
better visualization of the pars, foramen, facet joints, disk degeneration, spondylosis,
spondylolisthesis, and sagittal alignment. Flexion-extension views also are commonly
obtained to evaluate instability and flexibility. In the cervical spine, an open-mouth
odontoid view aids in evaluating for upper cervical spine injury, an oblique view can be
obtained to assess for foraminal stenosis of bony origin, and a swimmer view may
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
4/30

enhance visualization of the lower cervical spine. In the lumbar spine, an oblique view
may reveal spondylosis. Full-length spine radiographs are obtained on a 36-inch
cassette. A standing scoliosis radiograph is necessary in patients with a spinal deformity
to evaluate global alignment and associated coronal and sagittal imbalance. On a
standing lateral view, the femoral heads are included to allow for assessment of
spinopelvic parameters. EOS imaging is a more expensive and less available method of
capturing the entire skeleton. This enables visualization of lower extremity
compensatory mechanisms. Adjuncts to full-length spine radiographs, such as bending
and traction views, may afford additional information with regard to the flexibility of
spinal deformity.1,4,5
Computed Tomography
Advantages
Higher level of soft-tissue detail than conventional radiography and better bony detail than
MRI (Figure 2)
Greater sensitivity for traumatic injury than radiography
Rapid data acquisition
Additional detail of the occipitocervical junction and sacroiliac anatomy
Disadvantages
Relatively high levels of radiation exposure for patients
May underestimate ligamentous injury and spinal instability if osseous displacement is
absent
Sensitive to metal and motion artifact
Minimally used in pregnant women because of potential harm to the fetus
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
5/30

Figure 2 CT scans of the spine of a 55-year-old woman who sustained a burst fracture after
falling from a ladder. Sagittal (A) and axial (B) CT scans show an L1 superior end plate fracture
and an L2 burst fracture with posterior vertical laminar split. C, Sagittal CT scan shows
stabilization achieved via posterior instrumented fusion using ligamentotaxis. (Reproduced
from Yu E, Khan SN, Yu W: Spinal trauma, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic
Review, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014, pp 827-842.)
Additional techniques
CT myelography: invasive procedure involving the intrathecal injection of water-soluble
contrast medium to provide additional detail of compressive neurologic processes
Can be used if MRI is contraindicated
May lead to neural injury, cerebrospinal fluid leak, contrast reaction, meningitis, or seizure
CT angiography: intravenous contrast administration for evaluation of vascular structures
and identification of vascular injury

Computed Tomography
CT provides aggregated data from the rapid acquisition of multiple x-rays captured on a
circumferential detector.1,5,6 CT uses this large amount of data to provide better
anatomic detail than radiography alone. CT uses the Hounsfield scale (Hounsfield units)
to differentiate tissues based on radiodensity. The Hounsfield scale also can be used to
estimate osteoporosis.4
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
6/30

Plain radiographs may underestimate the amount of spinal trauma, and many trauma
centers have shifted to the use of CT for the evaluation of patients with traumatic injury
because of its improved sensitivity.7 Modern CT is performed considerably faster than
MRI. CT affords improved soft-tissue detail and resolution compared with plain
radiography but at the expense of a much higher dose of radiation.8 In addition, CT
affords better detail of osseous structures than MRI and, therefore, has become
increasing popular for evaluating bony anatomy.1 CT is particularly useful for
preoperative planning in patients with complex deformity, neoplasms, or nonunion and
in patients undergoing revision surgery. CT allows for better evaluation of areas in which
plain radiography cannot adequately capture anatomy, such as the occipitocervical
junction and the pelvis. In addition, the speed and detail afforded by CT has led to its use
for intraoperative navigation of instrumentation.
A major disadvantage of CT is the substantially higher levels of radiation exposure
compared with plain radiography. This limits the use of CT in pregnant women because
of potential harm to the fetus. CT also should be used judiciously in young children.
Although various windows may improve visualization of soft tissue, CT may
underestimate ligamentous injury and spinal instability if osseous displacement is
absent. CT is sensitive to metal and motion artifact.
Adjuncts to standard CT include myelography and angiography. CT myelography is an
adequate substitute for the evaluation of neural compression in patients in whom MRI
cannot be obtained because of pacemakers, defibrillators, and metal implants. A water-
soluble contrast medium is injected intrathecally, which identifies any changes to the
normal contour of the thecal sac because of compression. CT myelography is less
specific than MRI and may inadequately capture distal pathology if a block to the
contrast is present. The invasive nature of the intrathecal injection may lead to
headache, neurologic injury, cerebrospinal fluid leak, contrast reaction, meningitis, or
seizure. CT angiography involves intravenous contrast administration for evaluation of
vascular structures and identification of vascular injury. More commonly, contrast-
enhanced CT of the spine aids in identifying infectious and oncologic processes.1,4
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
7/30

Advantages
Provides high-resolution imaging, especially useful for evaluating neurologic compression
(Figure 3)
Noninvasive and does not result in harmful ionizing radiation exposure
Disadvantages
Expensive, time-consuming, and limited availability
Susceptible to motion and metal artifact
Contraindicated in patients with a pacemaker, defibrillator, stent material, or metallic debris
because of magnetic fields
Figure 3 Sagittal MRIs of a spine show hyperintense end plate changes at L4 and L5 on T1-
weighted imaging (A) and isointense to hyperintense end plate changes at L4 and L5 on T2-
weighted imaging (B) consistent with type 2 Modic end plate changes. (Reproduced from Hah RJ,
Alluri RK: Imaging of the spine, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 221-229.)

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
8/30

MRI involves the use of a strong magnetic field to produce oscillating radiofrequency
signals to excite tissues based on water molecule content.5,9 Tissues with a high quantity
of protons (muscle, ligaments) display a high signal intensity on MRI. Tissues with a low
quantity of protons (bone) display a low signal intensity on MRI. Various pulse sequences
are used to provide more specific anatomic detail. T1-weighted MRI affords a higher level
of anatomic detail. Tissues with high water content, such as cerebrospinal fluid, appear
dark or display a low signal intensity. Tissues with low water content, such as bone
marrow, fat, and contrast agents, appear bright or display a high signal intensity. T2-
weighted MRI often is obtained to identify pathology caused by the presence of edema
and higher water content in injured or pathologic tissues. Fluids such as cerebrospinal
fluid will display a high signal intensity on T2-weighted MRI. Fat-suppression MRI (short
tau inversion recovery) affords additional detail in patients with tumor, infection, or
ligamentous injury. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI aids in evaluating infection
and tumors and in distinguishing scarring from disk material after spine surgery.
The primary advantage of MRI is its high resolution for soft tissue, which makes it ideal
for evaluating neurologic compression. Dissimilar to CT and radiography, MRI does not
result in any harmful ionizing radiation. Several disadvantages of MRI makes it
prohibitive as a first-line diagnostic imaging modality. MRI is expensive, time-consuming,
and limited in availability. In addition, MRI is susceptible to motion and metal artifact,
which may substantially affect its resolution and use in patients with prior
instrumentation. Because MRI requires hours rather than minutes, patients who have
substantial anxiety, pain, or claustrophobia may require sedation to prevent motion
artifact. The use of magnetic fields during MRI limits its utility in patients with a
pacemaker, defibrillator, stent material, central nervous system clip, or metallic
debris.1,4
Systematic Approach for Evaluating MRI
A systematic approach to evaluating MRIs of the spine should begin with T2-weighted MRIs.5 We
recommend placing sagittal MRIs of interest next to axial MRIs, ensuring that cutlines are present
so the level of pathology can be identified. Starting centrally on the sagittal MRIs, we identify
sources of central spinal canal compression. We then move laterally to assess for lateral recess
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
9/30

and neuroforaminal narrowing. Next, axial MRIs are assessed to evaluate the cross-sectional area
of the thecal sac, cerebrospinal fluid flow, and spinal cord and nerve root impingement. T2-
weighted MRIs are then evaluated for areas of abnormal signal intensity and are correlated with
physical examination findings. In patients with trauma identified on radiographs or CT scans, the
integrity of the posterior elements should be assessed. Coronal MRIs should not be neglected, if
available, because coronal plane deformities and pathologies may only be seen on this view. T1-
weighted MRIs may be assessed to obtain additional anatomic detail and may be correlated with
abnormalities observed on T2-weighted MRIs. Other available specialized MRI pulse sequences,
such as rim-enhancement on T1-weighted gadolinium-enhanced MRIs, should be assessed to
better describe identified lesions. Short tau inversion recovery MRI may provide additional detail
with regard to the acuity of compression fractures. Radiographic findings must be correlated with
physical examination findings to make a diagnosis and plan management.
Bone Scintigraphy
Technetium Tc-99m–labeled phosphate is the agent most often used.
Commonly identifies osteoblastic processes, such as stress fractures, neoplastic processes,
infection, and bone metabolizing diseases
Infrequently used in the assessment of spinal pathology but may help identify pathologic
processes of osseous remodeling, such as spondylolysis

Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scintigraphy, which also is known as radionuclide bone scanning, involves the use
of radioactive materials administered intravenously or orally. The emitted radiation is
identified by external detectors to create anatomic reconstructions. Technetium Tc-99m–
labeled phosphate is the agent most often used. Bone scintigraphy commonly identifies
osteoblastic processes, such as stress fractures, neoplastic processes, infection, and
bone metabolizing diseases.1,5 Bone scintigraphy is infrequently used in the assessment
of spinal pathology but may help identify pathologic processes of osseous remodeling of
the entire skeleton, such as spondylolysis and metastatic lesions. Surgeons must
recognize that bone scintigraphy is not sensitive to oncologic processes that do not
involve osteoblastic activity, such as myeloma (Resource 1; Figure 4).

metastatic disease involving the bone. (Reproduced with permission from Jacob Babu,
MD, Baltimore, MD; Bo Zhang, MD, Baltimore, MD; and Amit Jain, MD, Baltimore, MD.)
Clinical Scenarios
Trauma
Imaging is unnecessary for awake/alert patients with no back or neck pain or tenderness who
are not intoxicated, do not have a distracting injury, and are neurologically intact.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
11/30

Conventional radiography: AP, lateral, and open-mouth odontoid views (for the cervical spine)
are useful for initial screening (must have adequate radiographs).
Flexion-extension views are an option if plain radiographs are unremarkable but may result
in instability-related neurologic injury.
CT: more sensitive at identifying trauma than plain radiography alone; often the primary
imaging modality for polytrauma patients.
MRI: performed if concern for an unstable spine injury exists and to evaluate the posterior
ligamentous complex (PLC); also indicated if neurologic injury is present to evaluate for
compressive etiology (hematoma, disk herniation, bony cord compression).
Evaluate T2-weighted MRIs for signal intensity at the PLC and T1-weighted MRIs for
ligamentous continuity to determine the status of the PLC.
Angiography: CT angiography or magnetic resonance angiography may be considered in
patients with signs and symptoms of vertebral artery injury and involvement of the transverse
foramen.

Trauma
Patients who sustain trauma should be carefully evaluated via appropriate imaging. In
particular, cervical spine trauma, if missed, may result in unrecoverable complications. In
addition, patients with a cervical spine injury have a 20% risk for noncontiguous spinal
injury, necessitating evaluation of the entire spine.10 Regardless, imaging is unnecessary
for awake/alert patients with no back or neck pain or tenderness who are not
intoxicated, do not have a distracting injury, and are neurologically intact. These patients
may be cleared of cervical spine immobilization. Otherwise, an initial radiographic
screening, including AP, lateral, and open-mouth odontoid views of the cervical spine, is
required. To assess cervical spine alignment, four parallel lines should be identified: the
anterior vertebral line, posterior vertebral line, spinolaminar line, and posterior spinous
line. These lines should be smooth without step-off, following the continuous lordotic
cervical curve. Any deviation is suggestive of injury. AP and lateral radiographs of the
thoracic and lumbar spine should be obtained as indicated by symptoms. Flexion-
extension radiographs are an option if plain radiographs are unremarkable but may
result in instability-related neurologic injury; therefore, flexion-extension radiographs
are indicated only if suspicion of gross instability is low. CT is indicated in patients in
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
12/30

whom radiographs cannot be obtained or in whom visualization of the upper or lower
cervical spine is poor.
CT is more sensitive at identifying spinal trauma than plain radiography alone and often
is the primary imaging modality for polytrauma patients.11 For patients in whom bony
injury is suspected, CT is the preferred imaging modality, clearly delineating retropulsion
into the spinal canal, which may result in severe consequences. Thin-section CT also is
necessary for patients who sustain trauma involving ankylosing spondylitis because of
the high risk of occult fracture that may be missed on plain radiographs. Patients who
meet the Denver criteria should be evaluated via CT angiography. This includes patients
with arterial hemorrhage from the neck/nose/mouth, patients younger than 50 years
with cervical bruit, patients with expanding cervical hematoma, patients with a focal
neurologic deficit, patients with a neurologic examination incongruous with head CT
scans, and patients in whom a stroke is revealed via CT.12
MRI is performed if concern for an unstable spine injury exists and to evaluate the PLC.13
T2-weighted MRIs should be evaluated for signal intensity at the PLC, and T1-weighted
MRIs should be evaluated for ligamentous discontinuity,4 which may reveal PLC injury.
MRI also is necessary in patients with a neurologic injury to evaluate for compressive
etiology, such as hematoma, disk herniation, and bony retropulsion. Obtunded patients
with facet dislocations, patients in whom closed reduction fails, and patients with
neurologic deterioration during closed reduction also require MRI before open
reduction.14
Degenerative Processes of the Spine (Spondylosis)
Imaging begins with AP and lateral radiographs, with optional views including flexion-
extension and oblique radiographs.
If symptoms of neurologic compression are persistent, then MRI of the area of interest is
obtained. MRI may effectively reveal the location and source of compression (centrally or
laterally located).
Sources of degenerative compression may include congenital narrowing, bony instability,
intervertebral disk pathology, hypertrophied posterior elements, and ossification of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
13/30

ligamentous structures.
Degenerative disk disease
Narrowing of the disk space on plain radiographs
Vacuum phenomenon on CT scans may indicate advanced disk degeneration
Loss of hyperintensity on T2-weighted MRIs
Disk herniation
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating disk pathology.
Identify if paracentral or far lateral to correlate with specific nerve root impingement and
physical examination deficits
Lumbar stenosis
Can observe bony narrowing on radiographs or CT scans, consider whether a dynamic
component exists, and obtain flexion-extension radiographs to evaluate for
spondylolisthesis
Assess extent of neural element compression, effacement of cerebrospinal fluid, and spinal
cord signal changes on MRI

Degenerative Processes of the Spine (Spondylosis)
Patients with degenerative spine conditions should be selectively screened via imaging
studies. In general, patients with degenerative spine conditions should undergo
nonsurgical treatment for 6 weeks unless red-flag symptoms, which include neurologic
deficit, oncologic history, night pain, weight loss, fever, and chills, are present.2 If
symptoms persist, imaging begins with AP and lateral radiographs of the cervical and
lumbar spine. Radiographs may reveal spondylotic changes in the uncovertebral and
facet joints, osteophytes, disk space narrowing, and degenerative spondylolistheses or
scoliosis. Flexion-extension radiographs may be obtained to assess spinal instability,
especially changes in the central spinal canal space with motion, which may be present
in patients with spondylolisthesis. Oblique radiographs may further characterize
spondylotic changes and foraminal stenosis.
In patients with symptoms of neurologic compression, MRI is obtained of the area of
interest. MRI may effectively reveal the location and source of compression (centrally,
posterolaterally, or laterally located). MRI can be obtained to assess the extent of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
14/30

compression, effacement of cerebrospinal fluid, loss of perineural intraforaminal fat, and
spinal cord signal abnormalities. Sources of degenerative compression may include
congenital narrowing, bony instability, intervertebral disk pathology, hypertrophied
posterior elements, and ossification of ligamentous structures. Axial T2-weighted MRIs
are most useful in evaluating central and lateral recess stenosis, whereas sagittal T2-
weighted MRIs reveal foraminal stenosis. Although MRI is the preferred imaging modality
for evaluating neural compression, MRI findings do not always correlate with patient
symptoms.
In the cervical spine, relative central stenosis is defined as an AP spinal canal diameter of
less than 13 mm on lateral radiographs. Absolute stenosis occurs in patients with an AP
spinal canal diameter of less than 10 mm on lateral radiographs. A Torg-Pavlov ratio,
which is defined as the ratio of the spinal canal to the vertebral body on a lateral
radiograph, of less than 0.8 also is suggestive of central stenosis.15 This is uncommon in
the upper cervical spine because the spinal canal diameter progressively decreases in
the caudal direction. In the lumbar spine, a cross-sectional area of less than 100 mm2 on
axial CT scans or MRIs indicates central stenosis.
Degenerative disk disease may be observed as narrowing of the disk space on plain
radiographs. The vacuum phenomenon on CT scans, which is observed as air in the disk
space, may indicate advanced disk degeneration and mobility in that segment. On T2-
weighted MRIs, decreased water and proteoglycan content manifests as loss of disk
hyperintensity. MRI is the best imaging modality for assessing degenerative progression
at the end plates. Modic end plate changes describes the progression of involvement of
the end plates.16 Type 1 changes are observed as hypointense on T1-weighted MRIs and
hyperintense on T2-weighted MRIs, signaling marrow inflammation and edema. Type 2
changes are observed as hyperintense on T1-weighted MRIs and isointense or slightly
hyperintense on T2-weighted MRIs, indicating fatty replacement of marrow. Type 3
changes are observed as hypointense on T1- and T2-weighted MRIs, signaling trabecular
microfracture and sclerosis. Disk herniation is best evaluated via MRI, which identifies
whether the herniation is paracentral or far lateral to correlate with specific nerve root
impingement and physical examination deficits (Resource 2; Figures 5 and 6).

Often, in patients with dynamic motion, neuroforaminal narrowing and nerve root

Spinal Deformity
Obtain standing PA and lateral radiographs of the spine. PA radiographs allow for prone
positioning and surgical table positioning comparisons.
Important for assessment of global and regional radiographic parameters
Assess coronal and sagittal imbalance
Identify compensatory mechanisms in the spine and pelvis
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Imaging of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002021
19/30

Use the Cobb method for angular measurements
Evaluate for flexibility of curves with bending and traction radiographs
MRI is recommended for patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis who have an atypical,
left-sided thoracic curve; pathologic reflexes; hairy patches concerning for spina bifida; or
syndromic pathology.
MRI is recommended for pediatric or adult patients with spinal deformity who have symptoms
of nerve compression.
CT can be performed to evaluate for abnormal bony fusions and for planning appropriate
surgical approaches and osteotomies.

Spinal Deformity
Spinal deformity evaluation requires a global perspective of the spine. Standing PA and
lateral scoliosis radiographs of the spine should be obtained. PA radiographs allow for
prone positioning and surgical table positioning comparisons. This is important for
assessment of global and regional radiographic parameters, coronal and sagittal
imbalance, and compensatory mechanisms in the spine and pelvis. EOS imaging studies,
including the lower extremities, may reveal additional compensation at the hips and
knees. Commonly assessed parameters include coronal malalignment using the central
sacral vertical line, sagittal malalignment using the C7 sagittal vertical axis, and pelvic
incidence–lumbar lordosis mismatch. In adults with a spinal deformity, a sagittal
imbalance greater than 5 cm, a coronal imbalance greater than 4 cm, and pelvic
incidence–lumbar lordosis mismatch greater than 10° are associated with inferior
outcomes.17,18 Cobb measurements are used to evaluate regional curvature, including
scoliosis and kyphosis. Adjuncts, such as lateral bending, traction, and supine
radiographs, aid in determining curve flexibility for preoperative planning.
In addition to plain radiographs, MRI is recommended for patients with adolescent
idiopathic scoliosis who have an atypical, left-sided thoracic curve; pathologic reflexes;
hairy patch concerning for spinal dysraphism; and syndromic pathology.5 In addition,
MRI should be obtained in pediatric or adult patients with spinal deformity who have
symptoms of nerve compression. CT can be obtained in patients with complex

Neoplasm
Conventional radiography is the first-line imaging modality. Radiographic bony changes may
not be observed until as much as 40% bony erosion occurs.
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the preferred imaging modality. Full-length spine images should
be obtained to ensure all noncontiguous lesions are identified.
CT is particularly useful for evaluating osteoblastic processes and to assess the extent of bony
erosion. CT also aids in evaluating for osteoid osteoma.

Neoplasm
Patients with back pain who have a history of neoplasm or constitutional symptoms
require radiographic evaluation of the entire spine. Radiographic bony changes may not
be observed until as much as 40% bony erosion occurs.1 Plain radiographs may reveal
lytic or blastic changes and resultant compression fractures. Lung, thyroid, and renal
lesions usually are lytic, whereas prostate and breast cancer typically are blastic.
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the preferred imaging modality, defining the extent of
tumor and neural compression. Full-length spine images should be obtained to ensure
all noncontiguous lesions are identified. Neoplastic processes most often appear
hyperintense on T2-weighted MRIs and hypointense on T1-weighted MRIs. CT is
particularly useful for evaluating osteoblastic processes and to assess the extent of bony
erosion. CT also aids in evaluating for osteoid osteoma. Imaging findings can be used to
guide surgical decision making.19
Infection
Abnormal radiographic findings may not be observed until 2 to 3 weeks after the onset of the
disease process.

Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the entire spine is the preferred imaging modality to evaluate for

Infection
Infectious pathologies commonly encountered in the spine include osteodiscitis and
spinal epidural abscess. Abnormal radiographic findings, which may include paraspinal
soft-tissue swelling, narrowing of the disk space, end plate erosion, focal deformities
after chronic infection, and fusion in late stages, may not be observed for up to 8 weeks
after the onset of the disease process. If infection is suspected, gadolinium-enhanced
MRI of the entire spine is the preferred imaging modality to evaluate for osteodiscitis
and spinal epidural abscess. MRI is the most sensitive and specific imaging modality and
helps delineate osteomyelitis from tumor. Epidural abscesses, which may be a surgical
emergency, may appear hypointense on T1-weighted MRIs and hyperintense on T2-
weighted MRIs with gadolinium rim-enhancement. CT myelography should be obtained
in patients in whom an epidural abscess is suspected who cannot undergo MRI.
Vertebral osteomyelitis may be confused for a tumor or trauma because it commonly
appears hyperintense and hypointense on T2-weighted MRIs and T1-weighted MRIs,
respectively. Paraspinal soft-tissue and epidural inflammatory changes may be observed.
Bone scintigraphy should be considered in patients in whom an MRI cannot be obtained.
Because bone scintigraphy detects all osteoblastic activity, it is sensitive but not specific
for the detection of osteomyelitis. CT can be used for surgical planning and the
assessment of bony destruction.
Tuberculosis is a less common infectious presentation and may be suggested if vertebral
body compression and severe angular kyphosis are observed on radiographs. Dissimilar
to pyogenic infections, sparing of the disk space is present early in the disease process.
Similar to other infections, MRI is the preferred imaging modality, displaying a low signal
intensity in affected areas on T1-weighted MRIs and a high signal intensity in affected
areas on T2-weighted MRIs. Smooth-walled abscesses with septa also may be observed.

Postoperative infections may be highly morbid conditions and require prompt diagnosis
and management. Radiographs are less useful in patients with an acute infection.
Chronic infections may appear similar to osteodiscitis, with end plate erosion, loss of
disk space, and loosening of screws observed. CT can detect abscesses and other fluid
collections and is useful for evaluating hardware, bony erosion, and pseudoarthrosis.
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the most useful imaging modality to evaluate abscesses
and bony involvement. Enhancing fluid collections observed on MRIs are highly
suggestive of infection (Figures 9 and 10).

Postoperative Imaging
Conventional radiography is the most common imaging modality performed to evaluate
postoperative fusion status in patients who have undergone numerous spinal surgeries.
If concern for recurrent herniation after decompressive procedures exists, then gadolinium-
enhanced MRI is obtained to delineate surgical scarring from a re-herniated disk.
Evaluating for pseudarthrosis
Flexion-extension radiographs can be analyzed for any listhesis of fused segments or
splaying of posterior elements.
Thin-section CT is the preferred imaging modality to evaluate for pseudarthrosis.

Postoperative Imaging
Conventional AP and lateral radiographs are the most common imaging studies obtained
to evaluate postoperative alignment and fusion status. Typically, initial radiographs are

obtained intraoperatively or immediately postoperatively to assess hardware placement.
MRI should be obtained in patients with worsening neurologic function postoperatively,
evaluating for inadequate decompression, bony fragments, and compressive hematoma.
CT myelography is appropriate in patients in whom MRI visualization is limited by
hardware artifact. If concern for recurrent herniation after decompressive procedures
exists, then gadolinium-enhanced MRI is obtained to delineate surgical scarring, which
enhances with contrast, from a re-herniated disk, which does not enhance with
contrast.4 The painful neurologic entity of arachnoiditis may be observed as nerve root
clumping within the thecal sac on axial MRIs (Figure 11).Pseudarthrosis may present as
chronic pain, worsening alignment, or hardware failure. Evaluation begins with flexion-
extension radiographs, which can be analyzed for any listhesis of fused segments or
splaying of posterior elements.20 Cervical interspinous motion equal to or greater than 1
mm is the cutoff value for the detection of anterior cervical pseudarthrosis on flexion-
extension radiographs of the cervical spine.20 If radiographs are nondiagnostic, then
thin-section CT is the preferred imaging modality to evaluate for pseudarthrosis.
